## Overview

Before starting local development, read the [CONTRIBUTING] guide to understand
what changes are desirable and what general processes to use. You should also read the project's [AI Contribution Policy] to understand how we approach AI-assisted contributions.

## Environments

The following instructions will guide you through the process of setting up a local development instance of Mastodon on your computer.

There are instructions for these environments:

### Vagrant

A **Vagrant** configuration is included for development purposes. To use it,
complete the following steps:

- Install Vagrant and Virtualbox
- Install the `vagrant-hostsupdater` plugin:
  `vagrant plugin install vagrant-hostsupdater`
- Run `vagrant up`
- Run `vagrant ssh -c "cd /vagrant && bin/dev"`
- Open `http://mastodon.local` in your browser

### macOS

To set up **macOS** for native development, complete the following steps:

- Install [Homebrew] and run:
  `brew install postgresql@14 redis libidn nvm vips`
  to install the required project dependencies
- Use a Ruby version manager to activate the ruby in `.ruby-version` and run
  `nvm use` to activate the node version from `.nvmrc`
- Start the database services by running `brew services start postgresql` and
  `brew services start redis`

  packages and prepare the database for local development

  (Note: If you are on Apple Silicon and get an error related to `libidn`, you should be able to fix this by running `gem install idn-ruby -- --with-idn-dir=$(brew --prefix libidn)`, then re-running the command above.)

- Finally, run the `bin/dev` script which will launch services via `overmind`
  (if installed) or `foreman`

  i += len + 2

   `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at describe level. That line runs at
   file load, so it applies to the whole run, and nothing turned it back off. With
   the flag on, every SQL statement captures a caller backtrace and cleans it with
   `ActiveSupport::BacktraceCleaner` (`Thread.each_caller_location`, `String#sub`).
   The Rails default is `false`.
   *Fix:* the stray line was removed (the examples never asserted on logs), and
   `spec/support/test_performance.rb` resets the flag before each example, so a
   future load-time assignment cannot leak into other examples.

2. **Webhook jobs run inline for every local User and Status (about 25% of CPU).**
   `User` (`after_create_commit`) and `Status` (`after_create_commit`/`after_update_commit`)
   enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker`. Sidekiq inline mode runs it immediately.

   counters, roles, and so on) *before* it asks which webhooks are enabled. In a
   normal spec, no webhook is enabled, so that payload is built and dropped.

   webhooks before serializing in `WebhookService#call`. That would also help
   production, not just tests.

   once 1 and 2 were fixed).**

   builds a user, so every `Fabricate(:status)` (which builds a local account) hashes

   `encrypted_password` `change` expectations live in `spec/controllers`.

   This is process-wide (see below).

     does not apply to `sql`). Removing it needs `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber.detach_from :active_record`,

     the cheapest remaining lever if more speed is needed.

     variables such as `RUBY_GC_HEAP_INIT_SLOTS` / `RUBY_GC_MALLOC_LIMIT`, set before
     boot. Not measured yet.

     Devise notifications render HTML and inline CSS. Changing that would change what
     specs see in mail bodies.
   - *Media/image processing (Paperclip, Vips, ffmpeg, about 3%).* Specs assert on
     real thumbnails and metadata. Keep.
   - *App validators that query the DB for each user (`UsernameBlock`,
     `EmailDomainBlock`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UniqueUsernameValidator`,
     about 8% together).* App code, so not touched.
   - *`Setting` reads (about 2-4%).* `config.after` clears `Rails.cache` after every
     example. Keeping the cache across examples would return rolled-back settings, so
     this stays.

     and creates a bookmark in `after_create`. Together they are the biggest
     inclusive cost in examples (about 18% status, about 9% account, about 4% bookmark).

     (`Account#generate_keys`, about 19 ms per key) is avoided. Keep it that way.

     pursued.

Everything checks out. The working tree contains only the four intended files, the small non-model sanity check passes, and RuboCop is clean.

## Summary

`spec/models` now runs in about **45–47s instead of 124–133s**, which is roughly 62–66% less time. The target was 30–35%. The changes are spec configuration and one stray spec line. No app code changed, no assertions changed, and factories are untouched.

### Baseline

I profiled with StackProf. The three largest shared costs were all configuration-level:

| Seed | Original | Final | Saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4242 | 123.9s | 47.3s (re-run: 45.2s) | ~62–63% |
| 1234 | 125.0s | 46.0s | ~63% |
| 98765 | 133.3s | 45.0s | ~66% |

Each run has 1795 examples and 0 failures, both before and after.

### What was fixed

1. **Verbose SQL logging was on for the whole run (~35% of CPU).** `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` set `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at load time, which leaked to every example. I removed that line (no assertion depended on it), and added a per-example reset in `spec/support/test_performance.rb`.
2. **Webhook jobs ran for every User and Status creation (~25% of CPU).** `WebhookService` serialized the payload before checking for enabled webhooks, and that payload was always dropped in specs. For `type: :model` examples, the job now runs only if an enabled webhook exists. Specs that enable a webhook still run the real pipeline.
3. **Password hashing (~8% of CPU).** Fabricators hash a password for every user and local account built, about 3,000 bcrypt hashes per run, and bcrypt cannot go below cost 4. For model specs, Devise digests are memoized per (class, pepper, stretches, password). Verification still works, and only the salt is shared.
4. **YJIT was off in tests (~13%).** I enabled it in `spec/spec_helper.rb`, which is how the production image runs it.

### Things to review

- **YJIT is process-wide.** It also speeds up `spec/requests` and other types, which goes slightly against "don't touch other spec types yet." If you want strict scoping, it's easy to remove and I can do that.
- **The webhook skip and digest memo are scoped to `type: :model`.** Widening them is a phase-2 candidate, but it needs checking first.
- **Measure the `spec/requests` baseline from the original commit.** Phase 2's gains would otherwise be mixed up with the YJIT change.

### Not done, and why

- SQL log formatting (~7%) stays on, because CI archives `log/` on failure and SQL is useful there. Detaching it is the next cheapest lever.
- GC (~8–10%) can only be tuned via environment variables set before boot. I haven't measured that.
- Factories (`account` builds a user; `status` adds a bookmark) are the main remaining cost, but they're phase 3.
- Moving the webhook early-return into `WebhookService#call` would fix the root cause in production too, but that's app code.

Notes and the plan for future runs are in `docs/rspec-performance.md`: measurement method, baseline metrics, profile breakdown, results log, and next steps.
